newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: FOCUS-OPEC begins talks to lift oil price.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-OPEC begins talks to lift oil price.

text.p: OPEC began talks on production levels in Vienna on Wednesday with cartel linchpin Saudi Arabia reiterating that it wants to see higher oil prices.

But delegates were sceptical on whether the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries would succeed in getting its biggest quota violator, Venezuela, to curb excess supply and help achieve a stronger market.
Delegates forecast that a Saudi-backed majority would favour the expedient of a freeze of current quotas under the ceiling of 25 million barrels per day until year's end.

But Iran, with the Saudis' support, led a move to try to deal with the chronic quota violations by some of the 11 members, led by Venezuela, that have driven actual OPEC output up some two million barrels above the target.
Excess oil has already sent prices down to around $18 per barrel, from $25 at the end of 1996.
"Yes, we would like to see the price higher," Oil Minister Ali Naimi of Saudi Arabia told lobby reporters.

The 11 heads of delegation met in closed "consultative" working session in the luxury Vienna hotel suite of the cartel president, Abdullah al-Badri of Libya, varying a schedule that had proposed an opening plenary.
Indonesia's Ida Bagus Sudjana told reporters the private talks would address "quotas and the problem we face".

Venezuela's minister, Erwin Arrieta, was earlier called to a private session with Badri, Naimi and Gholamrezah Aghazadeh of Iran - which a Gulf delegate said was intended to "emphasise the need for quota compliance".
That sounded like OPEC parlance for a tongue lashing. But beyond that, OPEC has no mechanism to compel a sovereign state to honour its quotas.
Delegates said that Saudi Arabia was in no mood to threaten to turn up the taps on its huge spare capacity as a retaliatory measure.
"There is no warning," said a Gulf source who stressed that an appeal was being made to "common interest".
But Venezuela, in excess of its official allocation for some three years, is ready to argue that the entire quota system is flawed.
Petroleos de Venezuela, their state oil company, has said that OPEC should abandon quotas altogether and opt for a policy of expanding its share of the world market.
That view is also being aired among analysts of the market.
"OPEC is at risk of being an anachronism," says Geoff Pyne, an energy economist at UBS Ltd. "It is achieving the status of a gentlemen's club with almost no influence on oil prices."
"It's a fantasy world. The quota system is a mechanism for losing their share of the market".
Pyne argued that OPEC output curbs, albeit leaky, suffice to keep a floor under prices. But that ensures that others make money investing in new oil fields and poaching OPEC buyers.
